title: Incident tolerance, capacity & routing check-in with Novum Systems
summmary: Discovery focused on fallback policies, multi-region routing, and feasibility of Private vs Dedicated for low-latency transactional inference. Customer wants clear SLA tradeoffs and pilot scope.
topics: fallback policies and active-active vs active-passive
private deployment constraints and network egress
next_steps: Redwood: send tailored pilot plan + pricing by 2026-04-02
Novum: provide traffic profile and top 10 prompt templates by 2026-04-01
action_items: Maya Patel - Share SOC2 and security pack (incl. KMS integration notes) by 2026-04-02
Aaron Liu - Draft pilot benchmark plan (target 200 TPS peak, 50ms p50 target) by 2026-04-03
Ravi Menon - Export 7-day traffic histogram and cold-start windows by 2026-04-01
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-29 16:00 UTC · 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Aaron Liu (Redwood SE), Lena Torres (Novum Head of Platform), Ravi Menon (SRE), Priya Kapoor (Security), Zach (PM)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone for joining, appreciate you carving out time. Quick agenda — talk about how you think about tolerance to incidents, fallback behavior, and whether Dedicated or Private is necessary for your needs.
[00:28] Lena Torres: Yeah, hi, thanks. To give quick context, we run a low-latency inference path for auth and recommendation, about 120 TPS steady with 300 TPS bursts. We saw a couple of blips last quarter when our cloud provider had a zone fail. We want to understand options: hosted, Dedicated pool, or private VPC.
[01:05] Aaron Liu: Gotcha, and when you say "blips" — is that total outage, increased latencies, or errors in responses?
[01:13] Ravi Menon: Mostly latency spikes and some 5xxs when we hit cold starts on the model side and the network routing took us to a degraded region. Our SLO is 99.95 at 100ms p99 for the auth path.
[01:40] Maya Patel: Okay 99.95 at 100ms p99 is pretty tight — we should map that to redwood SLOs and discuss acceptable partial degradation. A few options: active-active multi-region with steering, hot standby in another region, or fallback to a smaller model to preserve availability.
[02:05] Priya Kapoor: Quick sec — from security side we need to validate data residency and key management. Private deployment is attractive for that reason, but there's operational overhead.
[02:35] Zach (PM): Also cost — dedicated GPU pools look pricey if we need hot spare across regions. We want a sense of economics: what's a reasonable tradeoff so we don't overprovision.
[03:00] Aaron Liu: Sure. High level: Hosted is fastest to start but shared capacity — we have capacity tiers and graceful fallback paths. Dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolation, and Private (VPC/on-prem) lets you control network egress and KMS but needs more ops. For multi-region routing: Redwood supports policy-based steering, region failover, and automatic fallback to compatible quantized or smaller model variants.
[03:45] Lena Torres: Can you give an example of a fallback policy? Like what happens if region A goes down?
[03:52] Aaron Liu: One pattern — active-active with traffic steering: keep 70/30 split, use health checks and automated failover to move 100% traffic in <60s. Another is active-passive: keep a hot standby region that can absorb traffic in ~45–90s depending on warming. For cost-sensitive workloads we can fallback to a smaller quantized model with slightly lower output fidelity but much lower cost and faster startup.
[04:34] Ravi Menon: That 45–90s range — that feels long for auth. We can't accept that for a couple percent of requests. Is there a way to get <10s cutover?
[04:45] Aaron Liu: For <10s you need warm pools in the standby region or streaming KV-prefetch caches replicated across regions. Warm pools keep a set of warm workers ready, which increases cost but achieves sub-10s cutover. Another approach is prefix caching and client-side retries with local short-circuit to a tiny deterministic fallback service.
[05:20] Priya Kapoor: Do you capture audit logs for failovers? Our compliance team expects an audit trail of region switches and model fallbacks.
[05:30] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood Console records per-request route decisions, model variant used, and timestamps for routing events. We can set retention and forward to your SIEM. We'll include that in the security pack.
[05:52] [00:06:00] Lena Torres: There's also the question of correctness — smaller models may hallucinate more. For auth flows we need deterministic outputs — if we use fallback smaller models, what's the typical degradation?
[06:20] Aaron Liu: Good point. For deterministic flows we usually keep a very small policy model that only verifies tokens or runs a deterministic check rather than a full generative model. If you absolutely need 100% correctness, the fallback should be a synchronous pass-through to a cached decision or DB-based check.
[06:52] Ravi Menon: Our traffic pattern: ~70% short prompts (<=64 tokens), 25% medium (64–256), 5% long. Cold starts were triggered because of a spike of long requests after nightly batch jobs. We think if we can prewarm for the long tail we'll avoid many incidents.
[07:20] Aaron Liu: Prewarming based on traffic profiles works well. Redwood's autoscaler can keep a small pool warm during known windows, and we can do predictive prewarming based on your histogram.
[07:48] Zach (PM): What about model kv cache? If I failover to another region, the KV cache is cold and responses slow down — is there replication?
[07:58] Aaron Liu: KV cache isn't automatically synchronously replicated across regions in current runtime; we replicate keys asynchronously or use shared cache tiers. For strict low-latency auth, we'd recommend either active-active with synchronized cache or design fallbacks that avoid heavy KV-dependence.
[08:20] Priya Kapoor: On private deploy: network constraints — can Redwood run inside our VPC with private link? And how do you handle egress?
[08:31] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer VPC and private link peering. Egress is under your control; you can route through your NAT or we can support egress restrictions. Key management supports AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM integrations for on-prem.
[08:58] Lena Torres: Any SLA differences between Hosted and Dedicated?
[09:05] Aaron Liu: Hosted has published performance profiles but best-effort for isolation. Dedicated offers SLA-backed uptime and latency commitments tied to reserved capacity. Private has contractual SLAs depending on the deployment and support tier. We'll pull the exact SLA numbers in follow-up.
[09:35] Ravi Menon: For load shedding, do you offer circuit breaker patterns or token-bucket throttles at the route level?
[09:44] Aaron Liu: Yes, Redwood Console supports per-route throttles, token-bucket rate limits, and circuit-breaker policies that can return degraded responses or direct traffic to fallback models. You can also configure automatic fallback thresholds — e.g., if p99 latency > 200ms for 2 minutes then switch to fallback model.
[10:10] [00:11:30] Lena Torres: How often do you recommend running chaos drills? We run quarterly game days and want predictable behavior during experiments.
[10:22] Maya Patel: We recommend monthly tabletop + quarterly live drills for critical paths, and Redwood can help with synthetic traffic injection to validate fallbacks. We also provide tracing hooks you can wire into your incident playbooks.
[10:41] Zach (PM): On the economics — if we run warm pools in two regions, can you give a back-of-envelope on cost delta vs single region hot spare?
[10:52] Aaron Liu: Rough rule: hot pools across two regions generally add ~30–50% cost depending on size and utilization. Using smaller fallback models reduces that delta — e.g., keep a 2x smaller quantized model warm in standby region for ~20–30% extra cost but much smaller than full hot pool.
[11:20] Ravi Menon: Is there an option to only replicate auth route to Dedicated and leave other features on Hosted?
[11:29] Maya Patel: Yes, routing policies can pin specific routes to Dedicated capacity while other routes use Hosted. That hybrid approach is common — helps isolate critical flows while keeping general workloads on cost-effective hosted.
[11:52] [00:16:00] Priya Kapoor: Security question — during failover do logs or prompt content transit outside our tenancy? We need assurances prompts never leave our controlled network for private deploys.
[12:05] Aaron Liu: For Private, prompts stay within your VPC; for Dedicated, data is logically isolated but still under Redwood's managed infra. We can provide contractual language for prompt handling. For hosted, we have data usage policies and retention controls; we'll provide the doc.
[12:32] Lena Torres: Let's talk about acceptance criteria for pilot — we want to simulate region outage and observe failover behavior, measure failover time and impact on p99 latency, and validate that audit logs capture the change.
[12:45] Aaron Liu: That makes sense. Pilot steps: 1) baseline traffic replay, 2) configure routing and warm pools, 3) run a simulated regional outage, 4) measure impact and iterate. Target metrics: failover cutover < 30s for auth, p99 < 200ms during failover, and no silent data loss.
[13:18] Zach (PM): For the replay, we can share a traffic dump but need to sanitize PII.
[13:25] Ravi Menon: We'll scrub tokens and sensitive fields and share an anonymized sample.
[13:35] Maya Patel: Perfect. We'll also provide a pilot plan with required infra and a cost estimate.
[13:45] [00:25:00] Lena Torres: One more operational question — when a fallback happens and you switch to a smaller model, do you have a way to flag that responses are degraded so product can show a banner or change behavior?
[13:58] Aaron Liu: Yes, route-level signals are emitted and you can subscribe via webhooks or logs; we also provide a lightweight header in responses indicating fallback model and reason code so your app can surface it.
[14:20] Ravi Menon: Great. About monitoring — can Redwood push metrics to our Prometheus or do we pull from Console?
[14:28] Maya Patel: Both — we can push metrics to your endpoint or you can pull via API. We also provide OpenTelemetry-compatible traces that integrate with your stack.
[14:45] Priya Kapoor: For compliance, we need to see the results of your last penetration test and SOC2 type II.
[14:53] Maya Patel: Noted — action item to share SOC2 attestation and pen test summary.
[15:05] [00:30:00] Zach (PM): A minor nit — if the failover is to a smaller model that has a slightly different response shape, we need a compatibility layer. How disruptive is that?
[15:17] Aaron Liu: We recommend standardizing on a contract for the inference output; Redwood supports structured outputs and function-like responses so you can fall back to a model variant that preserves the schema. If the smaller model can't, we can insert a lightweight normalization step in the runtime.
[15:45] Lena Torres: I also want detail on SLA credits if Dedicated misses latency commitments during a failover scenario.
[15:55] Aaron Liu: SLA crediting depends on the contract tier — Dedicated SLAs cover uptime and latency windows outside of scheduled maintenance and force majeure. We'll surface the exact credit formula in the draft contract.
[16:12] Ravi Menon: Any limitations around private deployments in our eu-west region? We have data residency constraints.
[16:20] Maya Patel: We have private deployments in eu-west and can support region-specific deployments and KMS keys. We'll confirm regional availability in the follow-up.
[16:38] [00:36:00] Lena Torres: About diagnostics during an incident: what's the fastest way for our SREs to get access and collaborate with Redwood during a live failover?
[16:47] Aaron Liu: We offer shared troubleshooting sessions, runbooks, and cross-account read-only dashboards. For Dedicated customers we provide a dedicated Slack channel and optional rotation of Redwood on-call to coordinate.
[17:10] Zach (PM): If we do a mixed mode where auth is dedicated and recommendations hosted, is there added complexity for routing?
[17:18] Aaron Liu: Slightly — you'll need to define routing rules, but Redwood Console supports per-route policies and makes it straightforward. We can onboard with a config template.
[17:35] [00:41:00] Priya Kapoor: Any notable breach or incident history we should be aware of? We need transparency.
[17:44] Maya Patel: We maintain a summarized incident log and postmortems; we'll share relevant redacted items and our process.
[17:55] Lena Torres: Okay, recap for us — we need pilot plan, cost delta for warm pools vs fallback models, security pack, and a deep-dive with infra next week.
[18:08] Maya Patel: Agreed. We'll produce a one-page pilot plan and pricing estimate, attach security docs, and schedule the SE deep-dive.
[18:22] Aaron Liu: I'll lead the SE deep-dive and bring sample configs and a warm-pool sizing worksheet.
[18:30] [00:47:00] Lena Torres: Thanks all — this was useful. We'll get the traffic histograms to you by Friday.
[18:36] Maya Patel: Thanks, everyone. We'll follow up with next steps and the pilot artifact.

End of transcript.
